title: A charge selection rule fixes what a squeezed-light reservoir computer can compute and afford
abstract: Reading an optical quantum reservoir costs repetitions growing super-exponentially with feature order: what it can afford is set by its detector, not its optics. For reservoirs encoding data in a parametric pump's phase, one conservation law fixes what is readable and what it costs. Pairwise photon exchange conserves an integer phase charge: across an ensemble of input masks, order-D readout reaches exactly the assemblies of at most D unit-charge kernels; degree-one homodyne readout is universal for fading-memory functionals along weak-squeezing families, at shot cost polynomial in accuracy; and at fixed squeezing no finite degree reaches every sector, at a computable distance. Nonlinearity sits in the optics, not the detector, whose per-shot variance is fixed at every order. In a hardware-faithful digital twin-no device was built-the rule is visible: on an open RF corpus a displacement-encoded control at identical photon number loses 17.7 accuracy points, as the charge algebra predicts.
summary: This work establishes a fundamental 'charge selection rule' governing what a squeezed-light reservoir computer can compute and, crucially, what it can afford to measure. By deriving this rule from a conservation law, the authors show that the computational power is strictly limited by the detector's measurement order, not the optical complexity. This provides a powerful, resource-aware theoretical benchmark for quantum machine learning architectures.
main_problem: The paper determines the computational limits and, more critically, the measurement cost associated with using a squeezed-light reservoir computer.
main_result: A conservation law imposes a 'charge selection rule,' restricting the computable functionals to those spanned by at most D unit-charge kernels, while maintaining polynomial measurement cost.
method: The analysis uses a theoretical framework involving conservation laws derived from pair-wise photon exchange and is validated using a hardware-faithful digital twin simulation.
model_or_system: The system is an optical continuous-variable reservoir computer utilizing squeezed light, where data is encoded into the parametric pump's phase. The computation relies on the non-linear interaction and subsequent order-one homodyne readout.
key_observables: Charge (an integer conserved quantity), Normalized Mean Square Error (NMSE), and the achievable functional space spanned by unit-charge kernels.
important_parameters: The degree of readout (D), the squeezing parameter (r), and the shot cost (which is shown to be polynomial in accuracy).
main_assumptions: The readout is limited to order one, even though the dynamics generate higher-order correlations, and the analysis is based on a reduced single-loop model.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the selection rule organizing the function space by charge, comparing super-exponential moment estimator variance to the fixed order-one channel variance, and schematically detailing the measurement-economical reservoir components.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model, derives the conservation law leading to the selection rule, proves the exact characterization of the reachable functional space (Theorem 1), and demonstrates the computational advantage over simple linear filters.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, resource-aware characterization of quantum machine learning models, showing that physical constraints (like detector bandwidth) dictate computational power, which is highly relevant for quantum information processing.
